The ultimate total length recorded from extensive field surveys reaches 61 centimeters [Li = 61 centimeters], a figure that contrasts with the 40 centimeter value reported in some compilations. This considerable maximum length, paired with a slender, eel-like morphology, positions the species as the largest member of the pipefish family in the northeastern Atlantic. Sexual maturation in this species is timed to a specific body size rather than strictly to age, though both metrics are closely correlated under stable thermal conditions. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is 21 grams [Wwi = 21 grams], a mass that represents a substantial increase from the negligible hatchling weight. The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults reaches 0.79 grams [Wwp = 0.79 grams], a surprisingly low mass given the species' considerable length, which underscores its extremely slender body plan. This morphology, combined with a low reproductive rate, suggests that the species is adapted to habitats where food resources are predictable but not abundant.

Under these conditions, individuals have been observed to survive for approximately 2740 days [am = approximately 2740 days], or roughly seven and a half years, a considerable longevity for a fish of this body size at a temperature of 10.1 °C [T = 10.1 °C]. This extended lifespan, coupled with a delayed onset of reproduction at about two years, implies a relatively slow life-history pace that is more reminiscent of temperate seahorses than of most pipefishes. The long post-reproductive period observed in some individuals may be an artefact of captive conditions, but it also aligns with a strategy of repeated spawning over multiple seasons. Field records from the northeastern Atlantic, where water temperatures hover near this thermal regime, generally support this estimate, although predation pressure in the wild likely truncates the average survival time considerably.

When comparing the life-history traits of the Snake pipefish to those of related syngnathids, several distinctive patterns emerge. The ultimate total length of 61 centimeters [Li = 61 centimeters] far exceeds that of most congeners, yet the corresponding ultimate wet weight of 0.79 grams [Wwp = 0.79 grams] is strikingly low, reflecting an extreme elongation of the body without a proportional increase in girth. This morphology likely facilitates camouflage within eelgrass beds, a primary habitat for the species.
